rubric: PYTHON AS A FIRST LANGUAGE / FUNCTIONAL PROGRAMMING / CHAPTER 25

slides.title: Higher-order functions
slides.main: A function is a value like a number: pass it, store it, return it.

slides.title: A function is a value
slides.sub: A name without () is the function
slides.main: Parentheses decide: with them it is called, without them passed.

slides.title: Lambda
slides.main: A long lambda is a reason to write a named function.

body.text:
double = lambda x: x * 2
print(double(21))
print((lambda a, b: a + b)(2, 3))
print(sorted([3, 1, 2], key=lambda x: -x))
No return needed; the body is one expression: no assignments or blocks.

slides.title: Lambda and key
slides.sub: sorted, min and max take a key function
slides.main: Several criteria: a tuple key, the first is main, the second breaks ties.

body.text:
words = ["ccc", "a", "bb"]
print(sorted(words, key=lambda w: len(w)))
users = [{"name": "Anna", "age": 31}, {"name": "Boris", "age": 25}]
print(max(users, key=lambda u: u["age"])["name"])
pairs = [("b", 2), ("a", 2), ("c", 1)]
print(sorted(pairs, key=lambda p: (p[1], p[0])))
print(max([], default="empty"))

slides.title: map
slides.sub: Apply a function to each element, lazily
slides.main: map returns an iterator: wrap it in list or loop over it to see values.

body.text:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
print(list(map(str, nums)))
print(list(map(lambda x: x * 2, nums)))
print(list(map(lambda a, b: a + b, [1, 2], [10, 20])))
m = map(str, nums)
print(type(m).__name__, list(m), list(m))

slides.title: filter
slides.sub: Keep those for which the function is true
slides.main: filter(None, data) removes the empty: zeros, empty strings and lists, None.

body.text:
print(list(filter(lambda x: x > 0, [-1, 2, -3, 4])))
print(list(filter(None, [0, 1, "", "a", [], [0], None])))
print(list(filter(str.isalpha, ["abc", "a1", "xyz"])))

slides.title: map or a comprehension
slides.main: Ready function: map and filter; expression with conditions: comprehension.

body.text:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
print(list(map(lambda x: x * x, filter(lambda x: x % 2 == 0, nums))))
print([x * x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0])

cells.title: expression, condition
cells.sub: [x * x for x in a if ...]

slides.title: Fold
slides.main: For sum and max use built-ins; reduce is for rare folds.

body.text:
from functools import reduce

nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
print(sum(nums), max(nums))
print(reduce(lambda acc, x: acc * x, nums, 1))
print(reduce(lambda acc, x: acc + str(x), nums, ""))

slides.title: *args and **kwargs
slides.sub: Collect any arguments and pass them back
slides.main: This is how universal wrappers pass everything on without knowing what.

slides.title: Pure functions
slides.sub: Depend only on arguments, change nothing
slides.main: Effects at the edges, a pure core inside. Do not mutate others' arguments.

body.text:
def pure_add(items, x):
    return items + [x]          # a new list

def impure_add(items, x):
    items.append(x)             # mutates the argument

a = [1]
print(pure_add(a, 2), a)
impure_add(a, 2)
print(a)

def bad(x, acc=[]):             # one list for all calls
    acc.append(x)
    return acc

print(bad(1), bad(2))

slides.title: Composition
slides.main: Small transformations in a pipeline, each replaceable or movable.

slides.title: Common mistakes
slides.sub: Lambdas in loops and lazy map
slides.main: A lambda keeps the variable, not the value; map and filter return iterators.

body.text:
funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in funcs])      # all see the last i
funcs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in funcs])
print(len(map(str, [1, 2])))

[2, 2, 2]
[0, 1, 2]
TypeError: object of type 'map' has no len()

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: Functions are values; purity beats side effects; readability beats brevity.
